domain: Reads a 12-bit tile index from an EWRAM map table at 0x02020000 and copies a pair of palette-mapped colour halfwords from a lookup table at 0x02010000 into a VRAM-like destination at 0x06002800 + (a0<<11), writing to two rows 64 bytes apart, walking 11 steps along one axis (the a2-derived row/rowmod pair increments each step; the a1-derived col/colmod/parity values are held fixed for the whole call).
notes: compiler-families.json clustered this owner with template-main-0801e260 (ui/window/clear_tile_attributes_in_rect.c) at 8259 bp, but the real assembly shares none of that template's tile-attribute-clearing bit logic (no & 0x3FF mask, no RENDER_TILE_ATTR_OFS/RENDER_ALT_OFS access, no |=/&= clear). This is a family-clustering false positive (the n-gram/call-target signal is likely just the common 4-high-register push/pop prologue shared by many owners in this compiler's output), not a genuine template match. The template was not usable as a source-shape starting point for this owner.

Instead this owner's assembly closely matches the CopyEntry idiom already exact in games/gs1/src/map/render_palette_mapped_row.c and render_palette_mapped_column.c: same 0x02010000 colour-table base, same destination-row-doubling pattern (write, then write again 64 bytes later), same '(value/2) & mask' coarse index plus 'value & even-mask' fine destination-offset idiom. This owner appears to be a third sibling in that family (a block/run variant taking two coordinate-like parameters a1,a2 plus a bank selector a0), which is a genuinely useful lead for a future attempt, independent of the assigned template.

The retained candidate (this file) reconstructs the full three-parameter, 11-iteration loop with the CopyBlock(map, destination, parity) static helper and matches the reference instruction-for-instruction for the first 29 instructions (matched_prefix=29 in candidate-show --align) -- the entire parameter-decomposition prologue (sign-correcting halving of a1 and a2, the &0x7F coarse masks, the &30 fine masks, and the a1&1 parity bit) is byte-identical.

The remaining 41 differing halfwords are concentrated in two places: (1) the two wrap-around masks 0x3F80 and 0x3C0 used to re-mask 'row' and 'rowmod' after each += in the loop -- the reference materializes each via movs #imm8; lsls #N (e.g. movs r4,#254; lsls r4,r4,#6), while every source spelling tried here (bare hex literal, and a shift-of-immediate expression '254 << 6') makes this compiler emit a pc-relative ldr from the literal pool instead; and (2) the loop-invariant 0x02020000 map-table base, which the reference reloads from the literal pool on every iteration but which this candidate's compiler hoists into a callee-saved register outside the loop (changing several surrounding instructions to register+register indexed addressing instead of register+immediate).

rejected_experiments.experiment: declare row/col/rowmod/colmod/parity in flat top-to-bottom order (row, col, rowmod, colmod, parity) with the CopyBlock helper
rejected_experiments.result: worse (57 differing halfwords / 86 wrong instructions, still 172/172 bytes) -- the a1/2 sign-correction and the a2&30 rowmod computation get scheduled in the wrong relative order versus the reference, which visibly interleaves them (starts the a1 sign-correction, then computes a2&30, then finishes the a1 halving).

rejected_experiments.experiment: declare rowmod immediately after row (row, rowmod, col, colmod, parity), matching the reference's interleaved computation order
rejected_experiments.result: best result so far: 41 differing halfwords / 46 wrong instructions, matched_prefix=29. Retained as the candidate.

rejected_experiments.experiment: fully inline CopyBlock's body into the loop instead of calling a static helper
rejected_experiments.result: worse (82 differing halfwords / 74 wrong instructions, and candidate shrank to 160 bytes vs 172 reference) -- this compiler's inliner produces different addressing/scheduling than an explicit helper call for this owner; the helper-call form is closer to the reference.

rejected_experiments.experiment: give the two wrap masks (0x3F80, 0x3C0) their own named locals initialized via '0x7F << 7' / '30 << 5' or via '254 << 6' / '240 << 2' (mirroring the reference's exact immediate+shift bit pattern), instead of bare hex literals inline in the loop body
rejected_experiments.result: worse in both forms (86 and 92 differing halfwords respectively, candidate grew past 172 bytes) -- naming the masks as locals moves their materialization inside the loop body for this compiler instead of hoisting them out, which is worse than the bare-literal version's placement even though neither reaches the reference's movs+lsls encoding.
